title: The budget and the noisy source
short: 5 · The budget and the noisy source
oneLiner: An engineer installs a trojanized tool. The malware calls home to a known command-and-control (C2) server, the attacker moves to a build server, and starts stealing source code. The company's SIEM budget is capped at $15,000 a month.
teaching: At $2 per GB, indexing everything costs about $42,000 a month, so under the cap index-at-ingest has to stop collecting the noisiest logs: firewall and DNS. Tiered storage keeps them for a fraction of the cost, and detection-aware routing makes the suspicious ones useful in real time.

labels.rootCause: Jordan's laptop is running malware that calls home to cdn-telemetry-sync.example (203.0.113.80), a C2 server on the threat-intel feed. It arrived in a trojanized PDF converter installed at 08:52
labels.attackSummary: malware on Jordan's laptop is under an attacker's control
labels.hotEvidence: EDR shows the archive job on the build server, run by a service account that signed in from Jordan's laptop at 10:45
labels.ambiguousNote: Archiving source code on a build server could be a legitimate backup. The analyst checks EDR history and change tickets before deciding.
labels.objectiveImpact: 4 GB of source code for the company's routing software is now outside the network.
labels.undetected: No alert fired at any point.
labels.mitre: T1204.002 malicious file, T1071.001 web-protocol C2, T1021 remote services, T1560.001 archive via utility, T1567.002 exfiltration to cloud storage
labels.indicatorBlocked: the C2 server was blocked at DNS and the firewall
labels.containDone: Jordan's laptop and the servers it reached are isolated from the network; the stolen service-account password is reset
labels.blockDone: cdn-telemetry-sync.example and 203.0.113.80 blocked at DNS and the firewall
labels.scopeSearch: other machines talking to the C2 server
labels.scopeNoneLost: No other machine is still active.
labels.humanPivot: Pivots across EDR, identity logs, and the server's process history, one console at a time.
labels.confirmAsk: Tier-2 asks the build team whether the archive is expected
labels.playbook: SOAR isolates the machines from the network and resets the service-account password.
labels.rootMissingNote: Nobody can tell whether other machines are infected.
labels.rootSearch: DNS and firewall history for Jordan's laptop
labels.fullFinding: The agent also checks which other machines contacted the same server.
labels.fullPackage: isolate Jordan's laptop and any server it reached; reset the service-account password; block the C2 server at DNS and the firewall
labels.containPackage: isolate Jordan's laptop and the build server; reset the service-account password
labels.blockPackage: block the C2 server at DNS and the firewall
labels.pivotText: The C2 server was added to the feed yesterday, tagged as part of an active intrusion campaign.
labels.secondVictim: the C2 server was still reachable when another laptop got infected

events.title: Jordan signs in at the Chicago office
events.summary: A normal start to the day.

events.title: Jordan installs a trojanized PDF converter
events.summary: Downloaded from a lookalike site. It's unsigned, but EDR doesn't flag it: nothing matches a known signature.

events.title: The malware looks up its C2 server
events.summary: The laptop resolves cdn-telemetry-sync.example. That domain was added to the threat-intel feed yesterday.

events.title: First beacon to the C2 server
events.summary: An outbound HTTPS connection to 203.0.113.80, repeated every 5 minutes. The firewall allows it, because outbound HTTPS is normal.

events.title: Attacker starts exploring the network
events.summary: Hands-on-keyboard: lists file shares and finds a service-account password cached on the laptop.

events.title: Attacker moves to the build server
events.summary: Signs in with the stolen service-account password. The build server starts calling the same C2 server.

events.title: Alex installs the same PDF converter
events.summary: A second engineer finds the same lookalike site. Another laptop starts calling the C2 server. Nothing in EDR flags it.

events.title: Attacker packs 4 GB of source code into an archive
events.summary: On the build server, using a built-in archive tool.

events.title: 4 GB uploaded to external storage
events.summary: The archive leaves the network over HTTPS to a file-sharing service.

rules.name: Connection to a threat-intel-listed server
rules.logic: Outbound traffic to an IP address on the threat-intelligence feed.
rules.triageNote: The destination is on yesterday's threat-intel feed, and the laptop calls it every 5 minutes.
rules.agentTriageNote: Regular connections from one laptop to a known C2 server: active malware. Investigating.

rules.name: Large archive created on a server
rules.logic: A built-in archive tool compressing thousands of files on a server.
rules.triageNote: Could be a backup job, could be data theft. Needs a closer look.
rules.agentTriageNote: A 4 GB source-code archive, made by a service account that normally only runs builds and that signed in from an engineer's laptop at 10:45. High risk despite the medium severity. Investigating.

rules.name: Large upload to unfamiliar external storage
rules.logic: Gigabytes leaving the network to a file-sharing service never used before.

notes.enriched: The threat-intel match is what turns a routine outbound HTTPS connection into evidence.
notes.reduced: Removed: MAC address, TTL, packet ID, and other header fields nobody queries. The 12 identical beacons per hour become one record with a count.
